Vindication

/vin-dih-KAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Vindication means the clearing of someone from blame or doubt — the proof that a person or idea was right all along

Vindication means the clearing of someone from blame or doubt — the proof that a person or idea was right all along. For decades colleagues dismissed her theory about deep-sea vents, so the submersible's first footage felt like a complete vindication.

Worked Example

All season the critics jeered at the coach's unusual five-guard lineup, so the championship trophy felt like sweet vindication.

The coach was doubted and mocked, and the win proved his judgment had been right all along. Vindication is exactly that moment when doubt or blame collapses in the face of proof.

How Vindication Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

exoneration

exoneration: the official clearing of someone from a charge

justification

justification: proof that an action or belief was reasonable

validation

validation: confirmation that something is sound or true

Antonyms

incrimination

incrimination: being shown to be blameworthy

discredit

discredit: loss of trust in someone or something

How Strong Is It? — validation → vindication → exoneration

validation vs. vindication

validation vs. vindication: Validation is weaker than vindication — it is a mild, everyday confirmation that something works, with no accusation that needed defeating.

exoneration vs. vindication

exoneration vs. vindication: Exoneration is stronger than vindication — it is the full, official clearing of someone from formal charges, usually declared by a court or authority.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vindic

Root — vindic: to claim, defend, avenge (Latin vindicare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Latin vindicare meant 'to claim, defend, or avenge,' and -ation names the act or result — so a vindication is a successful defense: your name or your idea is claimed back from doubt.

Use the root in a new word: vindictive

Use the root in a new word: vindictive: Unlike his forgiving sister, Marco could be vindictive, nursing a grudge for years until he could repay it.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal

Vindication needs a backstory of blame or doubt: someone was accused, dismissed, or mocked, and then proof showed they were right — it even applies where no wrongdoing was ever alleged, as when a researcher's long-doubted theory is finally confirmed. Related but distinct: absolution (a word you may meet elsewhere in this unit) is the forgiving of guilt that really exists, while vindication is proof that the blame or doubt was never deserved.
